Looking for potential M&A targets and had a look at STLLR Gold. Tried to apply lessons learned and putting my neck out to see what the classroom thinks.
Assets:
1.Main asset Tower - Timmins camp, 4Moz M&I, 7Moz inferred. Geology and style similar to several historic mines in the area. Metallurgy: suggests 93% recovery. Overall grade is not the highest (0.8 for the open pits, 2 g/t underground), but currently expanding the open pit Jonpol deposit with >6 g/t.
2.Hollinger, Timmins: this is old tailings, low hanging fruit, low capex, limited in scale. Recovery ~60%. Progress is being made.
3.Colomac - 3Moz, and maybe even more interesting than Tower regarding grade and complexity, but it is out in the wilderness and not getting attention from the company
Management: CEO has worked and operated on several mines of similar geology, including in the same Timmins camp. VP Regulatory worked with government in Ontario do develop regulations within the same frame they now seek permitting for. VP Geology has not worked with Timmins-style geology, but was involved at Valentine which is similar. I'm not knowledgeable enough judge to his capabilities.
Valuation: share has doubled since low-point 2025, but still lower than it was 3 years ago. Market cap 240MCAD. Tower PEA shows NPV5% of >3000 MCAD at 3200 USD/oz gold, but Tower is many years from becoming a mine.
Cash position: recent financing providing 36MCAD, which is approximately what they burn in 18 months (of which most is exploration and "evaluation" whatever that is). Will need several rounds of financing.
Shareholders: Agnico has 11%, which in combination of hte size of the deposits is why I looked at it. Management has 3%, which is at least something. Eric Sprott has 15%.
Overall assessment
Pros: tier 1(?), excellent location, Agnico is a shareholder, valuation attractive, management ok as far as I can tell. Boring company name. cons: May have to wait 6-7 years before first pour from Tower. Will need more capital. Hollinger can potentially result in cashflow already late next year.
Given the evaluation and that Hollinger may start yielding cash flow while waiting for a potential take-over of Tower, I'm tempted. Maybe too early?

Key Minerals in Data Centers

Driven in part by compute-hungry AI, demand for data center capacity is growing which creates higher needs for energy and mineral resources to build, including critical minerals. The U.S. relies on imports from other countries for these key minerals.

1. Server boards and Circuitry

Server boards connect the essential electrical components of a server. These, and other intricate circuitry, require minerals that conduct well and resist corrosion, especially copper.

Estimated import reliance: Silver 64%, Gold 0%, Copper 45%, Tin 73%, Tantalum 100%, Palladium 36%, Platinum 85%.

2. Heat Sinks

Components that dissipate heat use metals that are highly conductive, malleable, and corrosion-resistant.

Import percentage: Aluminum 47%, Copper 45%.

3. Semiconductors and Microchips

Microchips and processors serve as data centers' "brains" which operate thanks to semiconductor materials such as Silicon and Germanium, that conduct electricity only under controlled conditions.

Estimated import shares: Arsenic 100%, Fluorspar (fluorite) 100%, Gallium 100%, Germanium 100%, Indium 100%, Palladium 36%, Platinum 85%, Silicon <50%, and Tantalum 100%.

4. Magnets and Data Storage
Specialized magnetic materials are used in hard disk and solid-state drives to store and retrieve data.

Minerals to be imported: Barite >75%, Boron 0%, Rare Earth Elements 80%


Energy Production: Beyond construction of data centers, additional mineral inputs are required for the energy generation and storage systems that power these energy-intensive facilities.

Sherritt enters term sheet with Gillon Capital amid Cuba sanctions pressure
Reuters
9:42 AM ET May-20-2026
May 20 (Reuters) - Canadian miner Sherritt International (SHERF.NaE) said on Wednesday it has entered into a non-binding term sheet, a preliminary agreement outlining deal terms, with U.S.-based Gillon Capital for a private placement of up to 55% of its common shares.
The placement involves a common share purchase warrant exercisable within nine months, with the exercise price expected to be at a discount to the C$0.11 closing price of Sherritt's (SHERF.NaE) common shares on May 15.
The nickel-cobalt miner said U.S. authorities do not oppose Gillon Capital's current talks with the company but any final deal will still require their approval.
Sherritt (SHERF.NaE) has come under mounting pressure from U.S. sanctions on its Cuba operations. Since January, the Trump administration has enforced what Sherritt (SHERF.NaE) has described as a de facto fuel blockade, threatened military action and expanded sanctions, forcing foreign businesses to leave the country.
On Tuesday, the Toronto-based company said it would not proceed with plans to dissolve its Cuban interests, including a joint venture with Nickel Company S.A., a state-owned Cuban nickel company.
The move reversed a decision announced earlier this month after the U.S. imposed sanctions on the joint venture.
(Reporting by Varun Sahay in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid)

China Dominates Rare Earths
Brazil, along with other countries with large reserves such as India, Vietnam, Sweden, and Norway, therefore wants to build its own value chains. Meteoric CEO Tunks points out that this requires staying power.
"In terms of mining, Brazil could become competitive relatively quickly," says Tunks. "But in production, it will still take some time."
Easier Extraction of Deposits
From a geological perspective, Brazil has an advantage compared to other countries with large reserves: According to the Brazilian Geological Institute (SBG), around 73% of the country's deposits consist of ionic clay soils.
"These are deposits where nature itself has taken over part of the processing process—granite rock that has altered or decomposed," explains Francisco Valdir Silveira, head of the SBG. "Ionic clay deposits are therefore easier to mine."
Geologist and mining entrepreneur Andrew Tunks sees further advantages for mining and processing rare earths in Brazil: "Processing requires a lot of electricity and water. Our mine in Brazil is powered 100% by renewable energy, and electricity is cheap. That's not the case in Australia. It's very dry there and electricity is very expensive."
Tunks hopes that the "gold rush" in Brazil will take a different course than in his home country: "In Australia, we extract huge quantities of raw materials and simply send them to China. We don't create a single cent of added value. I hope Brazil does better."
